Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 14:40: And what is said (Proverbs 28:14), "happy is the man who fears always" - our Rabbis, of blessed memory, explained (Berachot 60a) that this refers to words of Torah: they say, a certain student was walking behind Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosi, and he saw that he was fearful. He said to him: you are a sinner, for it is written (Isaiah 33:14), "the sinners in Zion are afraid." He said to him: but is it not written, "happy is the man who fears always"? [He replied:] that is written concerning words of Torah - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 14:41: And so one must fear in every place that has holiness, such as a synagogue and the like - as Jacob our father, peace be upon him, said when he saw the vision of the ladder (Genesis 28:17), "how awesome is this place! This is none other than the house of God" - meaning, it was not fitting that I sleep in it. And so King David, peace be upon him, said (II Samuel 6:9), "and David feared the LORD that day, and said, how shall the Ark of the LORD come to me?" - thinking that he was unfit, because of his own deeds, for the holiness of the Ark, and lest he not treat it with the holiness fitting for it, and blemish its honor. And along these lines David said (Psalms 5:8), "I will bow toward Your holy temple in fear of You" - and this is the meaning of "you shall fear My sanctuary" (cf. Leviticus 19:30).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 14:42: And so Rashbi, of blessed memory, explains (Zohar, Parashat Yitro 79b): it is taught, Rabbi Yosi said, one day I was standing before Rabbi Yehuda the Elder, and I asked him, what is meant by "and he feared, and said, how awesome" (Genesis 28:17) - what did he see, that he said it was awesome? He said to me: he saw the completeness of the holy faith that was present in that place, similar to what is above, and wherever completeness is present, it is called "awesome." I said to him: if so, why did they translate it [in the Targum] as "fear," not "completeness"? He said to me: there is no fear except in a place where completeness is present, and wherever completeness is present, it is called "awesome," as it is written (Psalms 34:10), "fear the LORD, His holy ones, for those who fear Him lack nothing" - implying that it says, "for there is no lack" - and in the place where there is no lack, completeness is present - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 14:43: According to his view, of blessed memory, the explanation of the verse "fear the LORD, His holy ones" is that the Name YHVH is complete, and you must fear it - and the proof of this is that those who fear Him are complete and lack nothing, because their fear of the Name brings them completeness. If so, it appears certainly that the Name YHVH is the source of completeness, and one must fear it; and from this we may infer, for every place where the Shechinah dwells, which is the collectivity of the ten [sefirot] included within YHVH, that it has completeness and one must fear it - this is the plain sense of the discourse.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 14:44: And when we expand the matter further, we may say that the place of completeness is the Holy One, blessed be He, together with His Shechinah - for the two of them together are a complete "Adam," since a male without a female is half a body and is deficient; and therefore, in every place where there is completeness, which is unity, fear dwells - as is known, that the place of fear is the Shechinah. And the root of essential fear is to ascend above all supernal things, "for He is great and ruling," and so on, as I explained, and it rests only upon a complete place, a properly established throne, as is known - and the essence of completeness is unity. Therefore it says, "he saw the completeness of the holy faith," which is the union of the whole of Atzilut with the Emanator, and therefore fear dwells there - and this is "fear the LORD," the Holy One, blessed be He, and His Shechinah.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 14:45: And it mentions fear specifically in [connection with] the Name YHVH, because in this Name the Cause of causes is unified; and therefore those who cleave to this Name and fear it lack nothing - for this Name is praised above all names and indicates complete unity, and within it the Cause of causes rests, as explained in the Gate of Fear, chapter 1, in the discourse we copied from the words of Rashbi from the Tikkunim. And therefore the verse speaks in the negative, "for there is no lack" - because the matter depends on the highest above, in a place where there is no deficiency of flow at all.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 14:46: And among the virtues of fear is what is said in the Tikkunim (page 5b), on the verse "fear the LORD, His holy ones, for there is no lack for those who fear Him" - it says: there will be no lack in his learning, and no lack in his soul, and no lack in his good deeds - for there is no poverty and lack like the lack of Torah and its commandments, as the masters of the Mishnah established, "there is no poor person except one lacking Torah and the commandments" - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 14:47: Further, concerning the virtue of fear, it says in the Midrash, on the verse (Proverbs 31:30), "grace is deceptive and beauty is vain," and so on, in these words: another interpretation, "grace is deceptive" - neither beauty nor wealth is accepted before the Holy One, blessed be He; what does He seek? Fear of sin, as it is said, "a woman who fears the LORD, she shall be praised." How much did Abraham our father, peace be upon him, do before the Holy One, blessed be He, and yet he was not praised for it - for what was he praised? That he feared sin, as it is said (Genesis 22:12), "now I know that you fear God" - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 14:48: And incidentally, we may understand what the matter of "fear of sin" has to do with the phrase "fears God," and what the matter of fear of sin is. Rather, the matter is understood through what our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said in Bereshit Rabbah concerning the Binding [of Isaac], in these words (56:7): "and he said, do not lay your hand upon the lad" - and where was the knife? Three tears fell from the ministering angels upon it and ruined the knife. [Abraham] said to Him: then what shall I do to him - shall I strangle him? He said to him: "do not lay your hand upon the lad." [Abraham] said to Him: shall I draw a drop of blood from him? He said to him: "do not do anything [me'umah] to him" - not even a blemish [mumah] - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 14:49: And the matter is: in all these alternatives, why did Abraham our father, peace be upon him, need to say, "shall I strangle him," "shall I draw blood from him" - why did he need this after the knife had already been ruined? Rather, it was because he feared sin, [thinking] perhaps I have some small sin that I was not careful about, [and therefore] my offering will not be accepted, since the knife was ruined. And along these lines of fear, it is written in the Sefer HaRokeach, in these words: "the root of fear is that it is difficult for him to do [what is required], and he abandons his desire and his inclination for the sake of the fear of the LORD, and he fears lest he not be wholehearted before the LORD like Abraham, of whom it is said, 'for you fear God' - for this is greater than [ordinary] trials" - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 14:50: And fear of sin applies even to a small sin; and therefore, in the Ra'aya Meheimna, "fear of sin" is explained as belonging to Binah, as we copied above at the end of chapter 3. And the matter is that the higher a person rises in level, the more exacting they are with him, along the lines of (Psalms 50:3), "and round about Him it is very tempestuous [nis'arah]." And its explanation is like the parable of servants serving the king: the king has many servants - some servants stand before him in the innermost chamber where the king himself is; others serve in the outer chamber further away; some are in his courtyard, some in his city, some outside his city - and all serve and all fear the king, but the closer one is, the more he fears, and the further one is, the more the fear diminishes from him; and those who are literally before him stand in dread and fear lest any error be found in them at all. Therefore it says, "and round about Him it is very tempestuous" - those who are literally around the King, it is very tempestuous for them; wherever "very" [me'od] is said, it is without measure - so it is explained in the Zohar, Parashat Va'era (page 27a).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 14:51: And so too, when the righteous man considers that he stands always before His providence, blessed be He, and that through the Cause of all causes, the Reason of all reasons, whose providence never ceases for a moment from all creatures - and he finds that he is "around the King" in the sense that the King has drawn him near to stand before Him, informing him of the secrets of His Heichal - and this is certainly from the side of the supernal soul given to the righteous man more than to the rest of the common people - he must fear lest the supernal King find in him some error, and the light of His providence and His flow be withheld from his soul and He grow distant from him, and then his soul is found blemished.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 14:52: And there is proof of this from what Rashbi says (Parashat Vayakhel, 217b), in these words: Rashbi said to his colleagues, you colleagues - behold, the Holy One, blessed be He, now delights in these words that are becoming crowns along that path, and you stand before your Master in your holy images; for I, at the hour I see you and gaze upon your images, see in you that you are marked with the secret of Adam, and I know that your image is prepared above. And thus the righteous are destined to be recognized before the eyes of all, and to show their holy countenance before the whole world - this is (Isaiah 61:14 [61:9]), "all who see them shall recognize them, that they are the seed the LORD has blessed." Meanwhile he saw Rabbi Yosi contemplating worldly matters. He said to him: Yosi, arise, complete your image, for you are missing one thing in yourself! Rabbi Yosi arose and rejoiced in words of Torah and stood with him; Rabbi Shimon gazed at him and said to him: Rabbi Yosi, now you are complete before the Ancient of Days, and your image is complete - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 14:53: And this is the level of supernal fear: that it should be in his eyes as though he always stood before the Cause of causes, for his image is engraved above in the secret of the soul, as we elaborated above in chapter 9. And if, Heaven forfend, he blemishes even through a mere thought, his soul is found blemished and distanced from the light of the countenance of the supernal King, as explained in the discourse I brought. And a person should consider how great his awe would be were he to stand before Rashbi, peace be upon him, who could recognize even a mere thought in a person's face, as explained - just as his colleagues stood in awe before him, for in standing before him they stood literally before the Shechinah. Correspondingly, a person must fear the Creator, who stands before him and knows his thoughts, as is known - and this is the matter of "and round about Him it is very tempestuous," which I explained.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 14:54: And to the extent that a person cleaves to his Creator and fears Him, so the Creator is found with him - along the lines of "if you seek Him, He will be found by you" (I Chronicles 28:9); and as we find that He was found with the ancients, that their prayer was heard immediately and their speech made an impression above - as it is said in the Zohar, Parashat Vayechi (218a), concerning the incident of Rabbi Yitzchak: the throne of his Master drew near through the wings of Rabbi Shimon; and likewise the incident of Choni HaMe'agel and many like him, found in the Gemara (Ta'anit, chapter 3).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 14:55: There is a sin that blemishes the ruach but does not blemish the nefesh, for according to the elevation of the ruach, so they are exacting with it; and so too there is something that will blemish the neshamah but not the ruach - such as being exacting about some commandment that was not performed with due precision. And the reason is that according to the fineness of the neshamah, so even a very light matter will blemish it - and this is called "fear of sin," and this is called "one who fears God," which is the supernal God who is in Binah.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 14:56: And the proof of this is what is said there in the discourse in Midrash Rabbah, after the discourse we copied above (Genesis 22:12), "for now I know that you fear God" - "now I know" to everyone that you love Me. And so in tractate Sotah (5:5) they explain that "fears God," said of Abraham, means out of love. And our Rabbis, of blessed memory, were compelled to say it was out of love because performing a commandment in darkness [privately] and with alacrity indicates love - and this we find with Abraham our father, peace be upon him (Genesis 22:3), "and Abraham arose early in the morning," and so on, "and saddled his donkey and took with him," and so on - behold, they compared this level of fear to love itself; and it is known that love is above, and although love is also found below, in the Shechinah, which is a "lesser love," its essence is above.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 14:57: And it is already possible to say that these are differing midrashic views: for the discourse on Proverbs, which interprets "fears God" as fear of sin, holds that this is below, in the Shechinah, where fear of sin also applies rightly; while Midrash Rabbah holds that "fears God" is above, in the place of love, as explained.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 14:58: And it is possible to say that the Shechinah is called "a woman who fears the LORD" from the side of Binah, along the lines explained in the Tikkunim (6a), that the Shechinah is called "fear" from the side of Gevurah - and now "fear of sin" applies correctly above, as explained in the Ra'aya Meheimna, and there [in Binah] is called "God" [Elohim], and from there the fear is drawn down below.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 14:59: Further, we may say concerning the matter of "fear of sin" that "sin" [cheit] is a term meaning "deficiency," along the lines of (I Kings 1:21), "I and my son Solomon will be deficient [chata'im]." And the fear is that he fears lest the flow be diminished on his account - whether above, from Imma Ila'ah, that it withdraw from the children, or from Imma Tata'ah, that the flow from the six extremities be diminished, so that they will not flow to her - along the lines of what she says, "my mother's sons were angry with me" (Song of Songs 1:6), as explained in the Zohar (Tazria 45b, Acharei 59b).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 14:60: Further, we may say concerning the matter of "fear of sin" that fear applies not only to [avoiding actual] sin, but even in a [proper] deed - for he fears lest he not have fixed it, or not done all that was required of it, according to the full obligation of service to God, blessed be He, for His great kindnesses toward His creatures - as the pious author of Chovot HaLevavot elaborated (Gate of the Service of God, chapter 3). And this too is "sin" along the lines mentioned, meaning "deficiency" - that is, perhaps he fell short of the obligation of service placed upon him, as it should properly have been; for every person to whom the Holy One, blessed be He, has done good, whether in wisdom or in wealth, or has performed miracles for him, is obligated all the more to service, so that he not be ungrateful for the Creator's abundant kindnesses toward him. And this is learned from what the Holy One, blessed be He, rebuked Eli concerning his sons (I Samuel 2:27), "did I not clearly reveal Myself to the house of your father when they were in Egypt... and did I not choose him out of all the tribes of Israel," and so on.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:1: After we have spoken of the matter of fear and its distinctions, as we found in the words of Rashbi and the words of our Rabbis, of blessed memory, we said we would speak in this chapter of several particular things that one who fears [God] should do, so that his fear be recognizable in him.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:2: And the general rule is to be careful in all things that involve the honor of the LORD, and there is a relation between honor and fear, because we find two distinctions in the matter of fear: the first, fear from the side of "you shall not do," as is written in the Tikkunim (146b), "its fear is in the negative commandments" - and fear, without qualification, is not to transgress the commandments of the King. And there is a fear for the fulfillment of positive commandments, as it is written (Psalms 128:1), "happy is every one who fears the LORD, who walks in His ways," and it says (ibid. 112:1), "happy is the man who fears the LORD, who delights greatly in His commandments" - for if He commanded that a commandment be performed, and it is neglected and one refrains from fulfilling the King's command, he is punished - and this is certainly the way of reason. And so our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Menachot 41a), that at a time of divine wrath, we punish even for [neglecting] a positive commandment.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:3: And so too the manner of honor that we are obligated to give our Creator has these two aforementioned distinctions. The first, to honor Him because of fear of Him, and by this he restrains himself from doing the opposite of His will - and in support of this, King Solomon, peace be upon him, said (Proverbs 27:18), "and one who guards his master shall be honored." And it is known that all "guarding" is [in the category of] "you shall not do," as it is said (Eruvin 96a), wherever it says "guard yourself," "lest," or "not," it is only a negative commandment. And "one who guards his master" refers to the attribute by which He, blessed be He, is called Adonai; and since this person is careful in the honor of his Master, not to do the opposite of His will, it is fitting that he be honored in the World to Come - along the lines of "for those who honor Me I will honor" (I Samuel 2:30), which is explained in the Zohar, Parashat Vayelech (285a): those who honor Me in this world, I will honor in the World to Come.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:4: The second, to honor Him by performing His will and His commandments; and honor, without qualification, is in the category of "you shall do" - as our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said in tractate Kiddushin, first chapter (31b): our Rabbis taught, what is "reverence" [morah] and what is "honor" [kavod]? Reverence: he does not stand in his place, and does not sit in his place, and does not contradict his words, and does not tip the scale against him [in a dispute]. Honor: he feeds him and gives him drink, clothes him and covers him, brings him in and takes him out - to this point. And along these lines they explained in the Tikkunim (146b), "its honor is in the positive commandments" - and we copied this passage in the Gate of Fear, chapter 5.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:5: And what is found designated in the books of the Prophets and Writings concerning the matter of honor mostly indicates the category of "you shall do" - along the lines of (Isaiah 24:15), "therefore in the region of light, honor the LORD," and likewise "for those who honor Me I will honor" - several distinctions explained in the Zohar all indicate the category of "you shall do." And so too (ibid. 58:13), "and the holy day of the LORD honored" - and our Rabbis, of blessed memory, explained (Shabbat 119a) that this refers to Yom Kippur, on which there is no eating or drinking - "honor it with clean clothing." However, immediately following it, honor is found in the category of "you shall not do": "and you shall honor it by not doing your usual ways, from pursuing your business, or speaking of it."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:6: And so too, besides this, honor is found in the category of fear, along the lines of (Deuteronomy 28:58), "to fear this glorious and awesome Name" - it appears that His being "awesome" comes from the side of His being called "glorious" [nichbad, related to kavod]. And likewise the honor given to sages, to rise before them, comes from the side of fear - as our Rabbis, of blessed memory, explained the verse (Ecclesiastes 8:13), "but it shall not be well with the wicked," and so on, "because he does not fear before God" - as referring to one who does not rise before his teacher; in these words (Kiddushin 33b): Rabbi Elazar said, any Torah scholar who does not stand before his teacher is called wicked, and does not live long, and his learning does not endure with him, and is forgotten - "that it shall not be well with the wicked, and he shall not prolong his days like a shadow" - because "he does not fear before God." What is this "fear"? I do not know what it is; but when it says "you shall rise up, and you shall fear," you must say this "fear" refers to rising up - to this point. And the plain sense of the verse is: he will not prolong his days, like this shadow which departs immediately - and the reason he will not have "good," and so on, is because this wicked person does not fear God enough to rise before his teacher; and here explicitly is honor stemming from fear. And so they said in the Midrash (Bamidbar Rabbah 7:2) that concerning the Levites, who did not sin with the calf, it is said, "for those who honor Me I will honor."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:7: And since we find honor stemming from fear, we thought to explain, at the end of this Gate, the conditions of honor that we are obligated to give our Creator, and thereby it will be recognized that we fear Him. Both distinctions mentioned concerning honor exist above: the distinction of honor in the category of "you shall do" I already explained at the end of chapter 2 of this Gate, that Chochmah is called Kavod [Honor/Glory], because it serves through its thirty-two paths under Keter; and likewise Tiferet serves and performs the command of Abba and Imma - behold, the distinction of honor from the side of "you shall do."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:8: Further, honor is found from the side of fear, and this is the reason for the honoring of elders that we are commanded - it is said in the Idra of Naso (Zohar 131b), in these words: "and these are the thirteen adornments of the supernal, holy beard, the most hidden of the hidden, mighty, to break and subdue all decrees of judgment. Who sees the supernal, holy beard, the most hidden of the hidden, and is not put to shame by it? And therefore all its hairs are aged and mighty in their arrangements" - to this point. And in the Idra of Ha'azinu (289a) they designated the supernal Elder [Atik] by the name Kavod [Honor], in these words: "on the beard of the holy Ancient One hangs all the preciousness of everything - it is called the Fortune of everything; from that beard, fortune, the preciousness of all precious things," and so on - and it concludes: "therefore all preciousness of preciousness depends upon this fortune" - to this point. And since honor depends above, and there is the place of length of days, as is known - one who does not give honor to an elder or to his teacher, who is in the place of an elder, and has no fear to rise before him, will not live long. And [the verse] says "before God," and does not say "who does not fear God" - to hint at the aforementioned secret, along the lines of what Rashbi explains (Zohar, Parashat Terumah 171a) concerning the matter of "before the LORD."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:9: And along the plain sense, it is possible to be precise about "before God" - meaning, his teacher, who stands before the Shechinah, along the lines of "as the LORD lives, before whom I stand" (cf. I Kings 17:1), which our Rabbis, of blessed memory, explained (Midrash Shmuel 8) as meaning that he stood before Achiyah the Shilonite, his teacher - behold, there is a distinction of honor from the side of fear, even though it be in the category of "you shall do," as I explained.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:10: Therefore we thought to explain all the distinctions of honor found in the Torah, Prophets, and Writings pertaining to the practical duty to honor our Creator, and the other matters we were commanded to honor. The first thing we are obligated in is to honor His great Name, and through honoring His Name we honor Him, for He and His Name are altogether one thing; and the honor of His Name refers to the Name YHVH, and the other names for which the Name YHVH is the source, and one must treat them with honor - not to throw them away, and certainly not to erase them, for one who erases a holy name transgresses a negative commandment. And it is not only the honor of YHVH, but also ritual objects of holiness that must be treated with honor - the reason being that once holiness and supernal illumination rest upon those letters, holiness spreads to all those branches [related objects], and they must be treated with honor - and this is the reason that ritual objects of holiness require genizah [respectful burial/storage].
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:11: And this is the reason for the honor of a Torah scroll - for since it is known that the Torah is His Name, as explained in the Zohar several times (Va'etchanan 265b), and will be explained in its place; just as His Name is called "glorious," as it says, "to fear this glorious Name" - so too the Torah, which is His Name, must be honored, by rising before it; and a Torah scroll should be clothed in a fine mantle, just as a person is obligated to clothe his father, and so on. And this is the matter found in several places in the Writings (Psalms 29:2), "give to the LORD the honor of His Name," and many like it.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:12: And from this aspect one must treat with honor every square [Hebrew] script, even if it was not written with [specific] holiness [in mind] - the reason being that since these letters are the image of the twenty-two holy forms through which all the worlds were created, and the lower letters indicate the intellectual forms cleaving to the Divine, it is fitting to honor them; and if he finds them in the marketplace or in other disreputable places, he should store them away in a fitting place. And it is already said in the Sefer Chasidim (section 97) that a certain pious man was punished for not honoring loose pages of the prayer book that he found and not sewing them together; see there. And it seems to me that it is good to be careful, if one was reading and needed to interrupt for some reason, to close the book or cover it, out of honor for the Torah - for if it remains uncovered, water or some other dirt might fall upon it, as this happens many times.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:13: And the pious Rabbi Yosef Yavetz, peace be upon him, wrote on the Mishnah (Avot 4:6), "whoever honors the Torah, his own body is honored by people" - matters pertaining to the matter of honor we are discussing, and I have seen fit to copy them here for their great practical benefit; in these words: Rabbi Yehudah ibn Shoshan, of blessed memory, wrote the reason - that one should recognize in his mind its greatness and the preciousness of its glorious splendor, for gold and glass cannot be compared to it, and he should consider that it is called "the strength of the Holy One, blessed be He," as it is said (Psalms 132:8), "You and the ark of Your strength." And he should be exceedingly careful in the honor of the Torah itself, and in the honor of its sages, and in the honor of its books.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:14: Honor of the Torah itself - how so? To occupy oneself with it always with an eager soul, and to be exceedingly careful in honoring it itself, that one be clean, his hands and garments clean, and the place free of filth. And I have a quarrel with those who feign piety and recite hymns in the marketplaces and streets without concern for whether there is filth there; and if they answer me, how can one possibly leave one's house for the synagogue without [reciting words of] Torah - let him reflect, and that is enough for him. And further, know and recognize that for mere restraint from transgression, one is given reward as though he performed a commandment - and where is there a commandment as great and as lofty as trembling in one's whole body and limbs before mentioning the [divine] Name, and looking to see whether he is in a fitting place, thereby fulfilling the commandment, "the LORD your God shall you fear"? And it is written (Malachi 2:5), "and he feared Me, and was afraid before My Name."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:15: And when he says, in the order of the day, "Blessed is our God who created us for His honor and separated us from those who go astray" - let him say it calmly and with proper intention, like a person who saw a fiery furnace before him and was bound to be cast into it, but was saved and given dominion and greatness instead - what is the consuming fire? The false religion of the idol-worshippers. And what is the dominion and greatness? The Torah of truth.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:16: And so too he should act when he recites a blessing in public and listens to the prayer leader reading from the Torah - as it is written in the Zohar, that one who directs his intention at that hour, with his ears attentive and the eyes of his intellect open, is credited as though he had received it at Mount Sinai - and just as there was only one voice there, so it is fitting that it be now.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:17: Honor of its sages - how so? He should conduct himself with great honor and reverence toward them, like the reverence of Heaven - for their reverence is included within "the LORD your God shall you fear" - and he should fear them as one who sees the face of God, meaning as one who sees the face of the king and his judges and officers.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:18: Honor of its books - how so? One must beautify his books and place them and store them away in the most select place in his house, and cover them with a fine cloth; and just as people employ various devices, hanging boards in the air and placing food on them to protect it from mice and cats, so too one should act to guard the honor of Heaven [in this manner for his books]. And when he moves them, he should not move them like other utensils, but rather with honor and modesty, as one moves the king's garments in the king's presence, and he should not touch them except with clean hands. These matters are entrusted to the heart, and one who fears God fulfills them all.
